reason_for_coming.value: To follow a brother already keeping a tavern at the forks
reason_for_coming.note: The relationship is documented - 'John Miller, brother of Samuel, the landlord' - and the motive is this record's reading of a man arriving where his brother already was. Chain migration is the commonest reason anyone moved anywhere in this decade and it is almost never written down.

later_census.scan_disagreement: The page has since been read off the image and does NOT give the same household. Recovered workbook against the sheet: males 1 against 2; females 4 against 3; children under ten 2 against 3. Neither is deleted. The sheet is the senior reading — it is the record, and the workbook is a memory of the record — but the bridge to this person was built on the workbook's row, so the disagreement is shown rather than resolved here.

persons.note: ELECTED ONE OF THE FIVE FIRST TRUSTEES OF THE TOWN on 10 August 1833 with 20 of 28 votes, and Andreas notes that he 'being a candidate himself, refrained from voting' - so he is one of only two men in this parcel whose conduct at the poll is recorded. His brother Samuel Miller kept the tavern on the north bank at the forks and is not written as a household here, because Andreas's 1833 roster names him only in passing as 'Samuel, the landlord' and this project's miller_house record has the house 'past its innkeeping days' by the scene date. Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named' - a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, compiled fifty years after the fact. A YEAR off it is documented; a MONTH is not, and neither is anything about 1835. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Miller, John” (poll_1833_020, line 41); Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Miller, John” (tax_1833_074, line 126); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Miller, John” (poll_1834_072, line 241). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Miller' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

resident_research.evidence_for: Retrospective Chicago histories independently identify John Miller with the settlement's first tannery, built near the North Branch/forks in 1831. The exact name, unusual trade and site corroborate the profile without inventing a July 1835 residence.

persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PARTNER IN THE SETTLEMENT'S FIRST MANUFACTORY. Andreas: 'The only manufactory established at that early day was the rude shed called a tannery, near the Miller tavern, where John Miller and Benjamin Hall were tanning a few hides into a rough but endurable leather.' He signed the 1832 militia agreement.

research_note: THE SETTLEMENT'S FIRST FACTORY AND ITS TWO NAMED WORKMEN, in a household assembled from three passages - the roster, Bates's 1883 interview and Andreas's own summary of the settlement's industry. A TANNERY IS A POPULATION FACT AS WELL AS A BUILDING: it takes hides from the butchers (Archibald Clybourne has his own household here) and it supplies the saddlers at Lake and Canal (Goss & Cobb, also here), so three of this parcel's households are one supply chain. That is the sort of structure the inferred phase should be looking for when it decides which trades the town must have had.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.

address_later.value: res Indiana, bet Wolcott and N. Dearborn
address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Miller, Jacob, blacksmith, res Indiana, bet Wolcott and N. Dearborn [died March 16, 1890, aged 79.]'. It is evidence about 1843, written here as 1843's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: NOT READ BACK, BECAUSE SOMETHING BETTER ALREADY STANDS. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 prints an address against this name in 1843, and it is left where it is. An 1835 placement already stands: this household works at `miller_tannery`, and clause 2 says an attested 1835 placement always beats a door printed 8 years later. The later address stays on the record as 1843's evidence and moves nothing.
